target_claim: The constructive induction defines a decomposition procedure (strip edges from E one by one to reach an inclusion-minimal cut F, split G-F into components A and B, partition E\F into E_A and E_B, recurse) whose output is claimed to express any cut E as a disjoint union of minimal cuts (bonds) of the whole graph G; the lifting step claims a minimal cut of G[A] is a minimal cut of G.
source_quote:
However, a minimal cut in a subgraph like G[A] or G[B] is also a minimal cut in
the entire graph G.
test_sketch: Implement the procedure exactly as written (~60 lines): given graph G and cut E, greedily delete edges from E until an inclusion-minimal disconnecting subset F remains; compute components A, B of G-F; partition E\F by component; recurse on induced subgraphs; return the collected 'bonds'. Oracle (brute force, |V|<=12): for each returned set H, check H is a cut of the FULL graph G (removing H increases component count) and no proper subset of H is; check the sets are pairwise disjoint with union E. Input family: small graphs with E = all edges or other disconnecting sets that are not vertex-partition cuts. Failing instance: K3 (triangle a,b,c), E = {ab, bc, ca}. E disconnects K3, but bonds of K3 are exactly the 2-edge pairs and no single edge is a cut, so E cannot be a disjoint union of bonds. The procedure picks F = {ab, bc} (A = {a,c}, B = {b}), then returns E_A = {ca} as a 'minimal cut', yet removing ca alone leaves G connected -- the oracle flags H = {ca} as not a cut of G, refuting the quoted claim and the overall correctness claim on a size-3 input.
